237 459 Nizamabad Black Pottery Handicrafts Uttar Pradesh
Nizamabad, in Azamgarh District of Uttar Pradesh, is renowned for its black pottery.
One such different form that combines utility with a unique tradition of decoration is the Black Pottery from Nizamabad, Azamgarh District, Uttar Pradesh.
Nizamabad is a small town situated about 100km (62 miles) north of Varanasi
Nizamabad, a village in Uttar Pradesh's Azamgarh, about 80 km from Varanasi

The art of making this kind of pottery originated in the Kutch region of Gujarat.
It is believed to have been brought to Nizamabad during the reign of the Mughals.
In the mid-17th century Muslim invaders a ttacked this town, which was originally called Hanumantgarh (Hindu), changing the name to Nizamabad.
The town was called Hanumantgarh that was renamed by the invaders as Nizamabad.
Early in the 19th century one of its feudal rulers invited potters from Gujarat to come and live here in exchange for land.
The potters were asked to provide pots for pouring and holding wate r, and gradually the shapes of the pots became influenced by Muslim forms.
The hi ghly decorative silver inlay incorporated into the pottery here has developed through the influence of bidri metalwork brought in by the Muslims from Hyderabad.

According to historical accounts the art of black pottery came from Gujarat. The ancestors of the potters had accompanied Abdul Farah Nizamabadi to the village during the reign of Emperor Alamgarh, 400 years ago.
Over 300 years ago during the reign of Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, some clay potters from Kutch (Gujarat) had migrated to Azamgarh and settled at Nizamabad to earn living.
Surendra's ancestors came from Gujarat, he says, about 500 years back and settled in what is now Uttar Pradesh.
Like all crafts, there are no available records as to its origins.
It is usually said that the craft is more than 500 years old.

It is believed that black pottery took root in Nizamabad due to a qazi's efforts during the rule of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. The qazi brought the art and craft of black pottery from Kutch, Gujarat, where it was first developed.

We have been hearing from our elders that once a kaji sahib (judge) in the Mughal administration saw black pottery by the Prajapati community in Gujarat. He was so impressed by the work that he brought some artisans to Uttar Pradesh, gave them land for housing and agriculture
According to mythological beliefs, the feudal rulers, influenced by the Persian style, had called artisans to live in this city to make utensils, fruits.
Later, talented artisans discovered the technique of adding black color through ash and smoke, which brought fame to this craft.
In 1905, there is a certificate for good work given by the British for a product made from Azamgarh using the Naqqashi technique.
Traditionally, only Prajapatis were potters and the skill was passed on from one generation to another.
According to the local people, the Prajapati community has been making this pottery since the beginning.
Ram Jatan Ram Prajapati received the National Award for Master Craftsman from the Government of India in 2004.

The method of making as Ram Jatan rattles off with veritable ease saying, "come to Azamgarh and you can view it first hand." I am not so sure, but try to follow the process. I have seen the pots being made locally by another Azamgarh potter in Delhi.
said Sohit Kumar Prajapati, a state awardee of the craft
Present were craftsmen who were awardees Ram Jatan Ram Prajapati, Mrs Pushpa Devi and Sohit Kumar Prajapati.

In Nizamabad, potters dig out clay from ponds during the dry months of April and May and store it inside their houses for use throughout the year.
The potters procure the clay during the summer months and store it in their homes for use throughout the year.
The mud for the pots is brought from ponds.
The dry lumps of clay are beaten to a fine powder, water is added and the clay is wedged by foot and then by hand whilst re moving any stones and coarse material.
Their units have small pits into which the clay is filtered, mixed with water and left for some days. When it thickens, the clay is kneaded by feet or using machines to make it lump-free.
The clay has been soaking in water in the pit for some days and is now thick enough to be kneaded using feet
After about 15 minutes of kneading, a portion of the clay is lifted to a plain surface and further kneaded with hands to improve elasticity.
The mud is soaked in water and in a chakki or a stone grinder turned to make it fine.
The dry mud is powdered. It is sieved several times
The mud is then kneaded with water. Approximately 40 percent of water is added to the mix.
The craftsmen make articles out of clay which has a very fine texture and shapes very well to different forms on potter's wheels.
Most potters work with wheels that turn by the hand. Electric wheels are also used.
The object is shaped on the wheel and removed using a piece of thread. It is now dried in the sun.
the handmade pottery is partially dried in the sun to retain some moisture. It goes back on the wheel for 'kharat' or peeling off uneven surfaces.
A second round on the potter's wheel ensures removal, via scraping, of any anomalies in the shape
It is again turned on the wheel, smoothed using a cutter, burnished stone and a few other implements.
Thrown pots are dried and smoothed with ghont, a quartz river stone.

To get the glowing black glazed effect, the pottery is dipped into a slip made of clay, mixed with vegetable matter.
A pot is dipped in a thin liquid matter of clay mixed with a particular vegetable material.
The sheen is obtained by dipping it into a solution of clay, vegetable matter, dried, then rubbed with a vegetable oil and fired.
Kavis, a colour made using clay and water, is applied and the pottery is then left to dry.

The solution is made using a local peeli mithi or yellow mud which is similar to fueller's earth. To the solution apart from the peeli mithi, proportions of mango bark, natural leaves and caustic soda are added.
Designs are etched or painted, and the objects fired in ovens fuelled with cow dung.
The pottery then goes inside the bhatti (oven), which is then fully covered with cow dung cakes.
the articles are fired in enclosed kiln with rice husks

The pieces to be baked are stacked in an earthen pot and filled with wooden pieces, cow dung and saw dust in the empty spaces. The mouth of the pot is then sealed. This is then lowered into the woodfired kiln and allowed to bake.
Firing is done in an open kiln by placing dung cakes between the wares and covering the heap with straw and mud.
It is baked at 750[degrees]C for six to eight hours time.
The oven cools down after 10 to 12 hours and then pottery is removed.
A fuel-intensive method, which involves baking the clay pieces for about 15 days in the furnace or kiln or, aawan, as it is locally called, produces about 300 pieces.

Water is then applied, rubbed and applied again to ensure that the silvery powder sticks permanently on the carved design
To lend a glossy look to the products, some vessels are coated with lacquer when still hot.
The lacquer application enhances the black pottery's lustre while it is still hot from the kiln.
Double firing in an open kiln and a closed kiln is done for dishes and tea sets used as crockery.
The making of an object takes three to five days, irrespective of the number of pieces to be made.

The black colour of the pottery is the outcome of a clay slip and reduction firing.

The pottery's colour is primarily due to the purposefully created oxygen-free conditions of the kiln. Oxygen will turn the clay red; therefore, the potters ensure that the kilns are air-tight to achieve the desired results.

When the pottery is inside the oven, it is important to ensure that there is no scope for oxygen to enter and the heat level remains high. The presence of oxygen can turn the pottery red and it won't get the black colour
The smoke that is generated in the process imparts the black colour.
When the baking starts, the combustibles give out smoke which is trapped inside the earthen pot in which it is baked. This smoke imparts a jet black colour to the objects inside.

The craftsmen of Nizamabad Black pottery in Azamgarh district create an array of black pottery items that include Vases, Cups and Saucers (tea set), dinner set, Water Jugs, Plates, Jars, Flower Pots, tableware and other items.
The artisans make a wide variety of decorative and household pottery items like lamps, containers, vases, flower pots, plates, incense holders and statues of Hindu gods and goddesses.
The potters make tea-pots, sugar-bowls and other decorative articles. The earthen wares and statues of Gods and Goddesses particularly of Ganesh, Laxmi, Shiva, Durga and Saraswati are also made.
A special kind of water pots, which is called surahis in colloquial language, are one of the well admired pots of Nizamabad.
They stand out with their striking designs of flowing lines and floral patterns on the surface.
having various beautiful floral and geometric designs itched to it
The craftsmen create a special pitcher-like form which is designed with thick slip into a light relief.
A sharp tool is commonly used for engraving on the pot. This is commonly referred to as naqqashi. The designs used vary but mostly are done freehand sans any tracing.
The naqqashi done on the pottery is known by different names. There are more than 50 designs and many more are made. There are jhoomar, bel, paurani, laung, papal and more.
The motifs are derived from nature.
However, certain portions such as the spout or the handle are left out as they are cast separately and then attached to the body.

Some of the products are used customarily during weddings in the area (with the custom being that a newly married couple should decorate their rooftop with elephants and horses made of black terracotta).
It is also colloquially known as Bidri Work.
This technique draws inspiration from Bidri craft.
